newsitem.title: INDONESIA: Southeast Asian cocoa - prices mixed, supply tight.
newsitem.headline: Southeast Asian cocoa - prices mixed, supply tight.

text.p: Southeast Asian cocoa prices were mixed on Wednesday with Indonesian values easing in line with declines in New York overnight, although exporters were hunting for beans to fill contracts, traders said.
The supply situation in Malaysia, however, was comfortable as grinders relied mostly on imported beans following a poor harvest in the May-June period, the traders said.
"Some exporters (in Indonesia) are desperately looking for beans to cover business," said one trader from Ujung Pandang, capital of the key growing region of South Sulawesi.
"There is a ship waiting (in Ujung Pandang) for 2,000 tonnes and they are rushing to get beans," the trader added.
Despite the shortage, however, Indonesian prices track price movements in New York for direction.
Traders said supply remained tight and added that players were keeping a close watch on the weather ahead of the mid-crop or smaller harvest expected in September.
"The heavy rains in several growing areas have stopped and we are now experiencing hot and dry weather again," one trader said.
He added that he expected a smaller mid-crop harvest, which usually accounts for some 30 percent of total annual output.
The Indonesian Cocoa Association has forecast 1997 production at 319,000-330,000 tonnes, up 10 percent from 1996.

"I have been getting reports that dry weather coupled with poor maintenance of trees could result in a smaller mid-crop this year. But we have to wait for another month or so to be certain about the crop size," the trader added.
Traders said fair, average quality (FAQ) cocoa was quoted at 3,350-3,420 rupiah/kg in Ujung Pandang, against 3,400-3,450 rupiah on Tuesday and unchanged from a week ago.

They said the decline from Tuesday was in line with overnight falls in New York, where the September contract fell $17 a tonne to end at $1,483, while second-month December closed $17 lower at $1,529 pressured by speculative long liquidation.

Traders said players were also keeping an eye on the Indonesian currency, which had shed some seven percent over the last three weeks against the U.S. dollar following offshore speculative attacks, but had since stabilised.
In Malaysia, prices were mixed in quiet trade.
On Wednesday, the Malaysian Cocoa Board quoted the SMC 1A grade out of Tawau at 3,500 ringgit ($1,325) a tonne, down 35 ringgit from Tuesday but unchanged from a week ago.
The board quoted the SMC 1B grade ex-Tawau at 3,450 ringgit, down 17 ringgit from Tuesday but up 45 ringgit from a week ago.
Traders quoted the SMC 1A at 3,550 ringgit and the SMC 1B at between 3,470 and 3,480 ringgit a tonne a Wednesday.
"There's not been much excitement in the international market lately," said a trader. "Likewise, there's not much trading interest either in the local market."
He said the supply situation was comfortable as grinders were relying mostly on imported beans.
Supply of beans has been acutely short in Malaysia since a dry harvest for the April/May/June period, local traders said.
